content: Viruses, derived from the Latin word virus meaning toxin or poison, are submicroscopic infectious agents that cannot grow or reproduce outside a host cell. Each viral particle, or virion, is composed of genetic material (either DNA or RNA) encased in a protective protein coat called a capsid. The capsid can take on various shapes, ranging from simple helical and icosahedral forms to more complex structures with tails or envelopes. Viruses infect cellular life forms and are classified into animal, plant, and bacterial types based on the host they infect. Biologists debate whether viruses are living organisms. Some argue they are non-living because they lack cells and do not meet the criteria for life, while others describe them as entities at the edge of life due to their possession of genes and ability to evolve through natural selection. Viral infections in humans and animals typically trigger immune responses and can cause diseases. In many cases, the immune system eliminates the virus entirely. Antibiotics are ineffective against viruses, but antiviral drugs have been developed to treat life-threatening infections. Vaccines can provide lifelong immunity and prevent viral infections. The term virus was first used in English in 1392, referring to poison or harmful substances. The modern understanding of viruses as agents causing infectious diseases emerged in 1728, long before their discovery by Dmitry Ivanovsky in 1892. The adjective viral was introduced in 1948. Today, the term virus is used to describe biological viruses and metaphorically for other self-replicating entities, such as computer viruses. Viral diseases have affected humans for centuries. Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs depict evidence of polio, though its cause was unknown at the time. In the 10th century, Rhazes wrote about smallpox and measles, providing the first clear descriptions of these diseases. Avicenna, in the 11th century, discovered the contagious nature of diseases like tuberculosis and sexually transmitted infections, introducing quarantine as a method to limit their spread. During the Black Death in the 14th century, Ibn Khatima identified microorganisms as the cause of infectious diseases. Edward Jenner's observation of immunity to smallpox in milkmaids who had contracted cowpox led to the development of the smallpox vaccine in the late 18th century. The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1979 after extensive vaccination campaigns. In the late 19th century, Dmitry Ivanovsky used a porcelain filter to study the tobacco mosaic virus, proving that the infectious agent was not a bacterium. Martinus Beijerinck later coined the term virus and described it as a contagium vivum fluidum (soluble living germ). The first human virus identified was the yellow fever virus. In the early 20th century, bacteriophages were discovered, and electron microscopy provided the first visualizations of viruses. Wendell Stanley crystallized the tobacco mosaic virus in 1935, revealing its protein composition. Advances in virology, such as the ability to grow viruses in chicken eggs and animal cell cultures, have significantly improved our understanding of these agents. The origins of modern viruses remain unclear, with two main hypotheses proposed. Small viruses may have originated as fragments of nucleic acids from living organisms, while larger viruses may have evolved from parasitic cells that lost unnecessary genes over time. Viruses may represent a primitive form of self-replicating DNA and could be precursors to life as we know it. Other simpler infectious particles, such as viroids, satellites, and prions, further complicate the understanding of viral origins. Classifying viruses is challenging due to their lack of a fossil record and the debate over their status as living or non-living entities. The International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) has developed a classification system based on shared properties, such as the type of nucleic acid in their genomes. The Baltimore classification system, based on the mechanism of mRNA production, complements the ICTV system. Viruses are grouped into seven categories based on their replication strategies. Structurally, a virion consists of nucleic acid surrounded by a protein capsid, which may be enclosed in a lipid envelope derived from the host cell membrane. Capsid shapes vary and are used for morphological and antigenic distinction. Viral genomes exhibit remarkable diversity, with some being circular and others linear. RNA viruses often have segmented genomes, allowing for genetic reassortment, which can lead to the emergence of new viral strains. Viruses replicate by hijacking the host cell's machinery to produce multiple copies of themselves. Their life cycle typically involves attachment to host cell receptors, penetration, uncoating of the capsid, replication of the viral genome, assembly of new virions, and release from the host cell. DNA viruses often rely on host polymerases for replication, while RNA viruses use virally encoded RNA replicases. Reverse-transcribing viruses, such as retroviruses, use reverse transcriptase to convert RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host genome. Bacteriophages infect specific bacteria and rapidly produce new virions, often leading to cell lysis. The debate over whether viruses are alive continues, as they lack cellular structures and self-metabolism but possess genes and can evolve. Their self-assembly within host cells has implications for the study of the origin of life. Viruses cause a wide range of diseases, from the common cold and flu to severe illnesses like Ebola, AIDS, and SARS. Their ability to cause disease is described in terms of virulence. Some diseases, such as multiple sclerosis and chronic fatigue syndrome, are being investigated for potential viral causes. The role of viruses in psychiatric illnesses, such as those potentially linked to the Borna virus, remains controversial.
